strengths: Addresses a timely and practically important problem: reusing 'sunk' compute from smaller pretrained checkpoints to build larger models, with direct relevance to reducing LLM pretraining costs.

The interpositional vs. stacking layer-growth comparison is well motivated by an interesting empirical observation (characteristic layer-wise weight-norm trend across many converged models, both self-trained and popular open-source MoE models such as DeepSeek-V2, Qwen3, Mixtral, Hunyuan, dots.llm1, GroveMoE), lending some generality to the hypothesis.
The work is validated at genuinely large scale (17B -> 35B -> 70B, over 1T tokens), which is a substantial engineering effort rarely seen in growth-method papers that typically stay at small scale.

A reasonably systematic set of ablations is provided: depth vs width growth trade-offs, noise-injection scale for expert duplication, pre-norm vs post-norm stability analysis, and a dedicated study of growth timing relative to sunk cost.
Extensive appendix with full per-checkpoint evaluation tables, architecture/hyperparameter details, and dataset composition supports reproducibility of the reported numbers.

The finding that growth timing/sunk cost correlates with final performance, together with the heuristic that additional FLOPs should be on the same order as sunk cost, offers a practically useful guideline for practitioners deciding when to grow a checkpoint.
weaknesses: A critical baseline is missing: the paper never compares growing a checkpoint against simply continuing to train the *original, non-grown* model for the same extra FLOPs. Without this, it is unclear how much of the 'benefit of sunk cost' is due to growth itself versus the trivial fact that later checkpoints already have higher accuracy before any additional training (as shown by the 'Start acc' column in Table 1). This weakens the central claim that growth is the mechanism unlocking the sunk-cost value.

Nearly all quantitative claims (10.66% gain, 1% noise-injection improvement, sunk-cost correlations) appear to be based on single training runs per configuration at each scale, with no repeated seeds, confidence intervals, or significance testing—particularly concerning for small differences (e.g., ~1% accuracy gaps from noise level) and for the headline 70B result, which rests on one run per condition.

The core contribution is largely an empirical/engineering study rather than a new algorithmic idea: interpositional layer duplication and expert duplication with small Gaussian noise are incremental variations on existing stacking/upcycling techniques; the theoretical justification (weight-norm trend argument) is heuristic rather than rigorously connected to the function-preserving principle invoked in the paper.

No direct quantitative comparison to competing growth/upcycling baselines from the literature (e.g., LLaMA Pro block expansion, Sparse Upcycling, Drop-Upcycling, LEMON/LiGO) is provided beyond the authors' own stack-vs-interposition ablation, making it hard to judge how much better this framework is relative to prior art.

The learning-rate confound noted by the authors themselves (same constant LR used for all continued-training runs regardless of the checkpoint's position in its original schedule) likely biases results against late-checkpoint growth and complicates interpretation of the timing study.

Generalization is only demonstrated within one proprietary training pipeline/architecture family; while weight-norm patterns are shown for external models, no external model is actually grown and retrained to validate the method beyond the authors' own models.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: reusing the computational sunk-cost of already-converged (not early-stage) MoE checkpoints, rather than growing models still early in training as in prior work (Du et al., Wu et al.).

The empirical motivation for interpositional vs. stacking copying is reasonably well supported by a broad survey of layer-wise weight-norm patterns across many open-source MoE models (DeepSeek-V2, Qwen, Mixtral, Hunyuan, Dots, GroveMoE), lending some generality to the core structural observation.

The scale of the final validation experiment (17B→35B→70B over ~1T tokens) is unusually large for an academic-style ablation study and demonstrates the method is at least operationally feasible at scale.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility effort: detailed architecture, optimizer, dataset composition, and extensive per-checkpoint evaluation tables in the appendix.

The sunk-cost-vs-additional-budget analysis (figs 7-8) provides a useful practical heuristic (allocate additional FLOPs on the same order as sunk FLOPs) that could inform real training pipeline decisions.
weaknesses: The headline 70B result (+10.66%) is a single run combining sequential depth-then-width growth and is not decomposed/ablated at that scale against the individually validated choices (interposition vs stack, noise vs no-noise) made only at 3B/17B; the large-scale claim therefore rests on an unreplicated, confounded pipeline with no repeated trials or variance estimates.

The "training from scratch" baseline used for the central comparison (fig. 1, +10.66%) is not clearly matched in hyperparameters/LR schedule to the grown model; the paper itself notes that using the same post-growth LR schedule for differently-staged checkpoints is suboptimal (section 4.1), which undermines the fairness and robustness of the central sunk-cost correlation claim.

Downstream accuracy differences reported throughout (often 0.5-2 points on a 5-6 task average) are not accompanied by any variance/seed analysis; given known evaluation noise at these model scales, it is unclear how many of the comparative claims (e.g., noise std sweep, depth vs width) are statistically distinguishable from noise.

No direct experimental comparison against existing growth/upcycling baselines mentioned in related work (LLaMA Pro, Sparse Upcycling, LEMON, LiGO, MSG, Drop-Upcycling) — only qualitative discussion, so the actual performance advantage of the proposed method over prior alternatives is not empirically established.

The core technical novelty is incremental: interpositional layer duplication and Gaussian-noise-perturbed expert duplication are relatively straightforward extensions of well-known function-preserving growth and upcycling ideas; the "proof" referenced in Appendix C for function preservation is actually a qualitative, non-rigorous argument rather than a formal proof.

The proprietary/synthetic portion of the 1T-token training corpus (not fully specified) combined with reliance on large-scale industrial compute limits exact reproducibility by independent researchers, despite the stated intent to release code.

The timing/sunk-cost study (section 4) is conducted only on the 3B→6B setting; whether the strong positive correlation between sunk cost and final accuracy generalizes to the 17B→70B regime is asserted but not separately re-verified with the same systematic checkpoint sweep used at smaller scale.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: reusing the sunk computational cost of converged MoE checkpoints via structured model growth, rather than growing early-stage/undertrained models as in prior work.

The interposition vs. stacking comparison for depth growth is well-motivated by an empirical observation (characteristic monotonic layer-wise weight-norm trend) that is validated across many open-source MoE models (DeepSeek-V2, Qwen1.5-MoE, Mixtral, Hunyuan, Dots-LLM1, GroveMoE) in addition to the authors' own checkpoints, giving the hypothesis good external support.

Width growth with small Gaussian noise injection into duplicated experts is a simple, well-ablated technique (noise scale sweep in Fig. 4) that yields a clear and intuitive downstream accuracy improvement without destabilizing training.

The paper provides a genuinely large-scale validation (17B→35B→70B over >1T tokens), which is a substantial and valuable engineering effort rarely seen in growth literature, and demonstrates a non-trivial 10.66% accuracy gain over scratch training under matched additional FLOPs.

The sunk-cost timing analysis (fixed additional-budget and fixed total-budget experiments across 12+ checkpoints) is thorough and yields actionable practical guidance (allocate additional FLOPs on the same order as sunk FLOPs; prefer constant-LR-phase checkpoints for growth).
Good appendix transparency: full per-checkpoint evaluation tables are provided for nearly all experiments, aiding reproducibility and allowing readers to inspect variance in the raw numbers.

The function-preserving discussion (Appendix C) offers a plausible mechanistic explanation (pre-norm vs. post-norm residual structure) for why width growth is more stability-preserving than depth growth immediately after expansion.
weaknesses: No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported anywhere; downstream accuracy numbers fluctuate substantially step-to-step in the appendix tables (e.g., several-point swings between adjacent checkpoints), which raises concern that some of the reported differences (e.g., 1% gain from noise injection, interposition vs. stacking gaps) may be within the noise of evaluation/training variance rather than robust effects.

The 'sunk cost' correlation analysis is confounded with the learning-rate schedule: later checkpoints are also later in the warmup/constant/annealing schedule, and the paper itself notes the correlation weakens/behaves differently once checkpoints enter the annealing phase, but does not fully disentangle LR-phase effects from pure 'amount of training' effects.

Large-scale claims (70B result, 10.66% gain) rest on a single training run each for the grown model and scratch baseline, given the compute cost; this is understandable practically but limits the statistical confidence of the headline result.
Only one growth ordering (depth-then-width) is tested at the 70B scale; no ablation of width-then-depth or interleaved alternatives is provided to confirm orthogonality/order-independence claims.

Baselines are narrow: the paper compares primarily against training from scratch, but does not benchmark against other established upcycling/growth baselines (e.g., Sparse Upcycling, LLaMA Pro, Drop-Upcycling) under comparable settings, making it harder to contextualize the magnitude of improvement relative to prior art.

The downstream evaluation suite is relatively narrow (MMLU plus six QA/commonsense benchmarks) and omits code, math, or generation-quality evaluations, which could be particularly relevant for assessing whether growth preserves or enhances specialized capabilities.

Some figures (e.g., Fig. 5's dense multi-panel comparisons) are visually cluttered and could be clearer; a few quantitative claims (e.g., exact percentage improvements) are stated without confidence intervals, making precise interpretation difficult.

strengths: Large-scale empirical validation is rare and valuable: the paper scales its method to a 70B-parameter MoE model trained on 1T tokens, going well beyond the small-scale toy settings common in prior model-growth literature.

Systematic and well-designed ablations: the paper carefully isolates variables (growth factor k, noise scale for width growth, routing variants such as fixed E with variable top-k), and each ablation is backed by quantitative loss/accuracy curves.

The identification of a 'convergence boundary' (~1x Chinchilla-optimal FLOPs) at which interpositional growth begins to outperform stacking is a concrete, testable, and novel practical finding, supported by both loss/accuracy curves and correlated weight-norm analysis (Figure 4, 5, Table 1).

Thorough orthogonality analysis (Appendix E) using Adam first-moment cosine similarity, cumulative weight-delta divergence, and order-independence experiments at 12B scale, providing multiple corroborating pieces of evidence rather than a single metric.

The sunk-cost timing study (Section 4) is a genuinely useful practical contribution for practitioners deciding whether/when to grow an existing checkpoint, including guidance on matching additional FLOPs to sunk FLOPs magnitude.

Extensive documentation of hyperparameters, architecture, dataset composition, and full per-checkpoint evaluation tables in the appendix, which aids partial reproducibility despite proprietary training infrastructure.
weaknesses: Central large-scale results (70B model, 10.6% improvement claim) rest on single training runs without seeds/error bars, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains are statistically robust rather than run-to-run noise, especially given the very large investment required to repeat such experiments.

The scratch-training baseline used for the headline 10.6% comparison is not clearly shown to be equally well-tuned (e.g., learning-rate schedule, warmup) as the grown model's continued-training regime; differences in optimization setup could partially explain the gap rather than the growth technique alone.

No direct empirical comparison against existing model growth/upcycling baselines (e.g., LLaMA Pro-style stacking at comparable MoE scale, Komatsuzaki et al. sparse upcycling, or Liew et al. 2025 upcycling scaling laws) under matched compute budgets; comparisons to these methods are only discussed qualitatively in related work.

The theoretical grounding connecting the weight-norm monotonic pattern to 'healthy convergence' and to why interposition specifically preserves it is largely qualitative/heuristic, leaning on loosely related theoretical results (neural ODE regularization, DeepNet stability) without a rigorous derivation specific to the claimed phenomenon.

All experiments use a single proprietary architecture, tokenizer, and data mixture; generalizability of findings (e.g., noise-scale sensitivity, depth-vs-width growth trade-off) to other MoE designs (different routing, granularity, or expert-choice routing) is not empirically tested, only weight-norm patterns are checked against a few public checkpoints.

Data, code, and model checkpoints do not appear to be released, and the training corpus mixes proprietary/synthetic data, limiting the ability of the community to reproduce the large-scale results even in principle.

The 'sunk cost' framing, while a nice narrative device, mostly formalizes an intuitive expectation (models trained longer/more make better initializations); the paper's novel technical contribution is more precisely the two specific growth operators (interposition, noisy expert duplication) rather than the sunk-cost concept itself.

strengths: The empirical scope is large: experiments span 3B, 6B, 12B, 17B, 35B and 70B MoE models trained up to 1T tokens, which is rare for an academic-style study of model growth and gives some practical credibility to the findings.

The interpositional-vs-stacking comparison is intuitive and is supported by a plausible structural argument (layer-wise weight-norm monotonicity) that is checked against several open-source MoE checkpoints (Appendix A) as well as the authors' own models.

The noise-injection ablation for width growth (Figure 6, Appendix C) is a useful, concrete practical recommendation that differentiates this MoE-specific growth method from standard dense-to-MoE upcycling, which typically needs much larger noise.

The appendix contains a reasonably thorough set of secondary analyses (growth-factor robustness, routing-variant ablations, function-preserving discussion, Adam-moment/weight-delta orthogonality analysis) that attempt to substantiate the orthogonality claim between depth and width growth from multiple angles.

The topic (reusing sunk compute from converged checkpoints for MoE architectures) is practically relevant to industrial LLM pretraining pipelines and is under-explored relative to dense-model growth literature.
weaknesses: Nearly all key claims rest on single training runs with no seeds, confidence intervals, or repeated trials, despite the inherent stochasticity of LLM pretraining (data ordering, initialization, routing noise). The headline 10.6% improvement at 70B/1T tokens is a single-point comparison, and the paper gives no indication of the variance one would expect from re-running either the grown model or the from-scratch baseline, so it is hard to assess whether the reported gain is a real effect or within run-to-run noise.

The paper calls its timing analysis 'scaling laws analysis' in the abstract, but no functional scaling-law form (e.g., power-law fits relating sunk FLOPs, additional FLOPs, and loss/accuracy) is actually derived; the 'positive correlation' claims in Section 4 are qualitative/visual trends read off scatter plots and tables rather than fitted, falsifiable laws, which is a weaker form of evidence than the terminology suggests.

The mechanistic explanation for why interposition beats stacking (preservation of a monotonically increasing layer-norm trajectory, tied to a 'Chinchilla-optimal FLOPs' threshold) is derived almost entirely from one 3B model family and then generalized; the boundary condition (~1x Fc) is identified from a coarse sweep over only 4-5 checkpoints with no statistical testing, and the citations to neural-ODE/DeepNet theory are invoked as 'principled' support without any new theoretical derivation connecting those results to the specific MoE weight-norm phenomenon observed here.

Reproducibility is significantly limited: the large-scale pretraining corpus mixes proprietary 'synthetic data' and an unspecified 'filtered code' dataset, exact data mixture ratios/curricula are not given, no code or checkpoints are released, and architecture/hyperparameter details for the 70B run beyond Appendix F are sparse; independent replication of the central 70B/1T result is effectively impossible.

The from-scratch baselines used for 'fixed extra/total FLOPs' comparisons are not shown to be separately tuned (learning rate, warmup, batch size) for their own scale; if the baseline hyperparameters are inherited from the smaller base-model configuration rather than optimized for the larger scratch model, the comparison could understate scratch-training performance and overstate the advantage of growth.

Evaluation is limited to MMLU plus six multiple-choice/commonsense QA benchmarks; there is no evaluation of generation quality, instruction following, code (despite code being 640B tokens of the training mix), or safety/toxicity, which narrows the evidentiary basis for the claimed 'boosting LLM pre-training efficiency' at scale.

Novelty is incremental: interpositional copying, noise-perturbed expert duplication, and orthogonal combination of depth/width growth are relatively straightforward recombinations of existing ideas (LLaMA Pro stacking, sparse upcycling with noise, function-preserving growth); the paper's distinguishing claim (applying growth to MoE models and to deeply converged checkpoints) is a reasonable but modest extension rather than a fundamentally new technique, and no comparison is made against other established growth/upcycling baselines (e.g., LEMON, masked structural growth, drop-upcycling) at the large scale beyond the simple stacking baseline.

Given the large number of design choices explored (growth timing, noise scale, growth order, routing variants), there is considerable room for the final reported configuration to have been selected post hoc based on the single large-scale run, raising concern about selection/confirmation bias in the headline result.

strengths: Exceptionally thorough empirical validation across scales (3B→6B→12B and 17B→35B→70B with 1T tokens), which is rare for an academic-style study and substantially strengthens the practical credibility of the claims.

The core technical insight—that interpositional copying preserves the characteristic monotonic layer-wise weight-norm profile of converged models while stacking disrupts it—is well motivated, tied to a plausible theoretical account (neural-ODE/implicit regularization view of residual networks), and corroborated across many open-source MoE checkpoints (Appendix A) as well as controlled timing experiments (Figure 4-5) identifying a concrete 'convergence boundary' near 1x Chinchilla-optimal FLOPs.

The width-growth analysis (minimal noise injection to break expert symmetry while preserving router/expert weights) is a sensible and clearly differentiated contribution relative to prior high-noise MoE upcycling work, supported by a clean ablation over noise scales and a random-init control that isolates the mechanism.

Orthogonality between depth and width growth is not just asserted but empirically probed from multiple angles (order-independence at 12B, Adam first-moment cosine similarity, cumulative weight-delta divergence, per-layer/per-category breakdowns), which is a nice piece of mechanistic analysis supporting the compositional growth strategy.

The sunk-cost vs. growth-timing study (Section 4) provides a genuinely useful practical heuristic (additional FLOPs budget should be on the same order as sunk FLOPs) backed by a systematic sweep over 12+ checkpoints and both fixed-additional-budget and fixed-total-budget regimes.
Reproducibility is reasonably well supported: detailed architecture/hyperparameter tables, dataset composition, infrastructure details, and extensive per-step evaluation tables in the appendix.
weaknesses: Most headline numbers (e.g., the 10.6% gain at 70B, the convergence-boundary location) come from single training runs without seeds/error bars, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the central claims, especially at the largest and most expensive scale where only one run is feasible.

Comparisons are largely confined to internal baselines (stacking vs. interposition, scratch vs. growth); there is no direct empirical comparison against other established growth/upcycling methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., LLaMA Pro, Solar depth up-scaling, sparse upcycling with high noise, Drop-Upcycling), so the claimed superiority is not benchmarked against the actual competitive landscape.

The 'well-converged' threshold (~1x Chinchilla-optimal FLOPs) is derived primarily from the 3B model family; while the 17B experiments confirm interposition > stacking qualitatively, the quantitative boundary itself is not independently re-derived at larger scale, leaving some uncertainty about generality across architectures/sizes.

Evaluation relies solely on standard multiple-choice/knowledge benchmarks (MMLU, ARC, BoolQ, HellaSwag, etc.); no generation-quality, instruction-following, or safety-related evaluation is included, which limits insight into whether gains transfer to more realistic downstream use.

The explanation for the observed weight-norm trend as a 'structural signature of healthy convergence' leans on loosely connected theoretical results (ResNet-ODE regularization, deep-transformer stability) without a tight formal link specific to MoE layers, so the causal story remains somewhat informal/descriptive rather than rigorously established.

The scalability study (Section 5) only tests one specific growth schedule (17B→35B via depth, →70B via width, with fixed token allocations per stage); it does not explore whether alternative orderings, ratios, or more than two growth stages would change the conclusions at this scale, despite the orthogonality claims suggesting this might matter less than shown at smaller scale.
